reason: “See eye to eye” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and the borrowing is real, but it was adjudicated twelve verses earlier: Mosiah 15:29 transcribes Isaiah 52:8 whole. 16:1 is the same speaker reusing a phrase he has just recited, within one speech, which ADJUDICATING §4 assigns to recurrenceRefs. It is recorded on the accepted link at 16:1, where the phrase now sits inside a compound built from Revelation 14:6 and Romans 14:11.

A five-word narrative connective. John 18:1 is Jesus crossing the Cedron to Gethsemane; Mosiah 16:1 is Abinadi resuming after a pause. The Book of Mormon uses “after … had spoken these words” dozens of times as a paragraph marker. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

A real five-word run, and worth an entry because the gesture looks meaningful. It is not distinctive: the KJV has men and God stretching forth a hand throughout, and Matthew 12:49's gesture is toward the disciples to identify them as his family, which has no counterpart at Mosiah 16:1. The gesture there is a peroration's, and the verse's borrowings are in what he says, not what he does.
Four words of ordinary prophetic connective, used twice in this chapter and constantly in the corpus. No contact with John 16:4's subject.

Four function words. Matthew 24:14's clause is “and then shall the end come”, a statement about the completion of the gospel's preaching; Mosiah 16:2's is “and then shall the wicked be cast out”. The shared string carries nothing.

sharedText: of the Lord, therefore the Lord
reason: Six words that are three formulas end to end. 1 Kings 13:26 is the disobedient prophet killed by a lion; Mosiah 16:2 is the wicked not redeemed. The run exists because both sentences name the Lord twice in quick succession.

Four words, and “cause” means different things in the two verses — Proverbs 31:8 has a legal cause to be pleaded, Mosiah 16:3 has a cause in the sense of an origin. The verse's sources are Revelation 12:9, 2 Corinthians 11:3, James 3:15 and Genesis 3:5; see the four accepted links.

A tempting four-word run, because Matthew 1:21 is the naming of Jesus — “he shall save his people from their sins” — and Mosiah 16:4 reads “God redeemed his people from their lost and fallen state”. The shared words are a possessive, a preposition and a possessive; the verbs differ (save/redeem) and so do the objects (sins / a lost and fallen state), and the Book of Mormon's phrase “lost and fallen state” has no KJV source at all. Excluded as a resemblance of syntax with no shared content word.

The best exclusion in this chapter, because the string is a genuine five-word run and the KJV means something else by it every time. “Bands” in the King James Old Testament are the bands of a yoke — Leviticus 26:13's “I have broken the bands of your yoke, and made you go upright”, Ezekiel 34:27's identical phrase, Psalm 2:3's “let us break their bands asunder”. The KJV never speaks of the bands of death. That phrase is the Book of Mormon's own, coined in this speech (Mosiah 15:8, 15:9, 15:23, 16:7) and standard in the corpus thereafter, and it is one of the places where the text is manifestly composing rather than borrowing. The verse's actual New Testament source is 1 Corinthians 15:55, whose grave and victory and death and sting Mosiah 16:7 keeps in the KJV's own pairings; see the accepted link.

The same five-word run and the same yoke. Ezekiel 34:27 is the restoration of Israel to safety in their land; the bands broken are their servitude's. See the entry at Leviticus 26:13 for the full reason and for what “the bands of death” actually is.
Four function words. Job 12:14's clause is “there can be no opening”, of a man God has shut up; Mosiah 16:9's is “there can be no more death”, whose source is the KJV singleton at Revelation 21:4.

Five words, of which the operative one is “brought”. Ezekiel 21:7's idiom is “it shall be brought to pass”; Mosiah 16:10's is “shall be brought to stand before the bar of God”, a different construction with a different object. The verse's sources are 1 Corinthians 15:53 and Revelation 20:12.

Four words of a disjunctive formula. Ben-hadad's servants are guessing whether the Samaritans came out for peace or war. The construction at Mosiah 16:10 is Ecclesiastes 12:14's — “whether it be good, or whether it be evil”, which occurs in exactly two KJV verses and only there of a judgment — and it is recorded as a composite on the accepted Revelation 20:12 link.

Ranked first by the n-gram stream and verbally the nearest thing in the KJV: Judges 2:17 reads “and yet they would not hearken unto their judges”, and Mosiah 16:12 reads “and yet they would not depart from them”. The exclusion is made with the reason stated openly, because it is a judgment a reader may fairly reverse. The formula “and ye/they would not” occurs in five KJV verses and identifies no source on its own; what the catalogue has proposed instead is a scene rather than a string — arms extended twice and twice refused, which is Matthew 23:37's lament over Jerusalem and nowhere else in the Bible. If the scene is declined, Judges 2:17 does not become the source; the verse simply has none, since its distinctive phrase, “the arms of mercy”, is in no KJV verse. See the whyNot on the accepted link.

Four words, and the sense is inverted. Psalm 37:17's arms are the wicked's and they are broken; Mosiah 16:12's are mercy's and they are extended. The collocation “arms of mercy” occurs in no KJV verse and is one of the Book of Mormon's own coinages.
Four words of connective phrasing. Hosea's idols are made according to the craftsmen's own understanding; Mosiah's wicked go according to their own carnal wills. No content word is shared.

Four words spanning a clause boundary in both texts. Ezekiel is showing Israel the pattern of the house that they may be ashamed; Mosiah 16:12 is describing men warned of their iniquities who would not depart from them.

sharedText: a shadow of those things which are to come
reason: The KJV singleton “shadow of things to come” was adjudicated at Mosiah 13:10, where Abinadi first applies it — to his own execution — and it recurs at 13:31 and here. 16:14 is the same speaker's closing instruction to the priests, “if ye teach the law of Moses, also teach that it is a shadow of those things which are to come”, and it is his own formula by now rather than a fresh borrowing. Recorded on the 13:10 row's recurrenceRefs. Note that 16:14 is the one place he attaches the shadow to the law itself rather than to an event, which is Colossians 2:17's own referent — so the chapter ends by putting the borrowed phrase back where Paul had it.
Four function words. Mark 6:15 is the crowd guessing at Jesus's identity. Nothing is shared but the construction.

sharedText: shall see the salvation of the Lord
reason: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Isaiah 52:8 and 52:10 at this verse, and both references are sound as chapter-level pointers: Abinadi has just transcribed Isaiah 52:8-10 as Mosiah 15:29-31, and 16:1 restates it. The verbal link belongs elsewhere in both cases. Isaiah 52:10's own wording is at Mosiah 15:31, verbatim for twenty-nine words, and that is where the link sits. What 16:1 actually has is “all shall see the salvation of the Lord” — and Isaiah 52:10 reads “the salvation of our God”, not “of the Lord”. The phrase Mosiah 16:1 uses occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 14:13 and 2 Chronicles 20:17, and the catalogue puts the link there (CONVENTIONS §6a: our reading governs, and the link goes where the wording is). The register sends a reader from 16:1 to Mosiah 15:31 for Hardy's Isaiah and to the Exodus 14:13 row for the wording.
